artworks.title: Fly agaric
artworks.description: A fungi painting from 1890 showing growing sophistication in rendering texture

artworks.title: Velvet Shank
artworks.description: Depicts fungi at full growth during winter with tiered clusters, transitioning from dark velvet to creamy pale-yellow and golden-orange caps

artworks.title: Old man of the woods
artworks.description: Depicts Strobilomyces strobilaceus fungus that resembles a pinecone

artworks.title: Parrot Toadstool
artworks.description: Small fungi with vivid green waxy cap, showing longitudinal cross-sections revealing yellow-green gills, painted in 1894

artworks.title: Spike Cap mushroom
artworks.description: Depicts Gomphidius glutinosus with round, slimy, purple head, easy to spot among moss

artworks.title: A Dream of Toasted Cheese
artworks.description: Thank-you card for Uncle Henry showing industrious mice in science lab, one reading chemistry textbook with NH3 reference

artworks.title: Red Riding Hood meets the Wolf
artworks.description: Features mushrooms in the foreground right, incorporating Potter's mycology knowledge

artworks.title: Toads' Tea Party
artworks.description: Features personified toadstool mushrooms used as seats for frogs

artworks.title: Dalguise gardens
artworks.description: Painting created in 1875 showing the back gardens in a self-made sketchbook

locations.name: Dalguise House, Perthshire, Scotland

locations.name: Armitt Museum

locations.name: Perth Museum
locations.significance: Received 25 fungi drawings by Potter in Charles McIntosh's 1922 bequest

locations.name: Eastwood in Dunkeld, Scotland
locations.significance: First stay in 1893 where mycology was Potter's main focus; location where she found rare fungi

locations.name: Lennel House near Coldstream

locations.name: Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew

locations.name: Heath Park
locations.significance: Potter's holiday home where first meeting with Charles McIntosh occurred on October 29, 1892

trueFalse.statement: Beatrix Potter referred to Scotland as 'home sweet home' in her memories of childhood.
trueFalse.correction: She specifically remembered Dalguise in Perthshire, saying 'I remember every stone, every tree, the scent of heather... oh, it was always beautiful, home sweet home.'

trueFalse.statement: Charles McIntosh was a doctor who mentored Beatrix Potter in mycology.
trueFalse.correction: Charles McIntosh was a postman who became an expert on fungi after losing fingers in a sawmill accident, not a doctor.

trueFalse.statement: Brothers Grimm, Hans Christian Anderson, and Aesop authored stories Potter heard from nurse Anne McKenzie.
trueFalse.correction: These authors' stories were read to Beatrix and her brother during their childhood in Scotland.

trueFalse.statement: Potter painted the picture letter with Peter Rabbit for Eric Moore.
trueFalse.correction: The picture letter featuring Flopsy, Mopsy, Cottontail, and Peter was sent to Noel Moore, not Eric Moore.

trueFalse.statement: The Perth Museum received 25 fungi drawings by Potter in 1922 through Charles McIntosh's bequest.
trueFalse.correction: These drawings were later positively attributed to Potter in 1978 by Scottish mycologist Dr. Mary Noble.

trueFalse.statement: Potter's fungi research paper was immediately published by the Linnean Society.
trueFalse.correction: George Massee presented it to the Linnean Society but reported it needed more work; Potter never revised it.

trueFalse.statement: Potter made two copies of fungi sketches - one for Charles McIntosh and one to keep.
trueFalse.correction: She would typically make two copies after Charles shared specimens with her, and also wrote letters about them.

trueFalse.statement: The painting Fly agaric from 1890 demonstrates Potter's skill in rendering color.
trueFalse.correction: The painting demonstrates Potter's growing sophistication in rendering texture, not color specifically.

trueFalse.statement: Potter's holidays in Scotland ended by the 1900s but the memories stayed with her forever.
trueFalse.correction: Her approach to illustrations, memories of people and country, and folklore from Nurse McKenzie stayed with her.

trueFalse.statement: Charles McIntosh gave Potter harsh criticism about her fungi drawings.
trueFalse.correction: Charles McIntosh provided gentle feedback and mentorship to Potter throughout their friendship.

trueFalse.statement: The Latin name for Old man of the woods fungus references its similarity to a pinecone.
trueFalse.correction: Strobilomyces strobilaceus references the fungus's visual similarity to a pinecone.

trueFalse.statement: Boletuses were among Potter's favorite types of fungi.
trueFalse.correction: She loved their viscous caps, smooth undersides in place of gills, blue bruising effects, and thick bulging stems.

trueFalse.statement: Charles McIntosh advised Potter to create detailed pictures and cross-sections of the same fungi.
trueFalse.correction: This artistic advice helped her provide more detail of fungi's unique characteristics.

trueFalse.statement: Potter thought the Lennel House was terrible despite the honeysuckle and roses.
trueFalse.correction: Despite disarray and disrepair, she noted flowers bloomed and overall liked the place and its fresh air.

trueFalse.statement: Potter sketched fossils from many angles using dotted lines and arrows, advice from Charles McIntosh.
trueFalse.correction: This technique was given to Beatrix from Charles McIntosh in relation to fungi studies.

trueFalse.statement: Potter arranged Bucklerbury excavation tools by classification and inventory number.
trueFalse.correction: She arranged them by varying type, size, and medium to make a pleasing arrangement to the eye.

trueFalse.statement: William Turner Thiselton-Dyer was the director at Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew.
trueFalse.correction: He was described as a thin, elderly gentleman with a dry, cynical manner who disregarded Potter.

trueFalse.statement: Potter continued scientific research and revised her fungi paper before 1898.
trueFalse.correction: While she continued research through 1898, she never revised her paper and gradually replaced science with storytelling.

trueFalse.statement: Potter predicted her fungi illustrations would be in a book, which came true 70 years later.
trueFalse.correction: W.P.K. Findlay used 59 illustrations for the fungi volume of Wayside and Woodland series in 1967.

trueFalse.statement: Potter stopped all artistic work during her years of scientific research and fungi sketching.
trueFalse.correction: She continued to illustrate tales, sketch characters, send gift booklets to publishers, and make picture letters.
